title: Claims against the government, cities, police and public bodies

items.title: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019
items.says: The Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019 binds the Ontario government (the Crown).

source.expect: This Act binds the Crown

review.problem: Section 2 (1) only says the Act binds the Crown; the description of what the whole Act covers (liability, immunities, notice, procedure) is not in s. 2.

items.title: The old Proceedings Against the Crown Act (history only)
items.says: The Proceedings Against the Crown Act, as it read before its repeal, still applies to cases started against the Crown before the 2019 Act came into force, except that section 11 of the 2019 Act (including its ending of some claims and dismissal of some cases) applies to those older cases too. A case started on or after that day follows the 2019 Act, no matter when the facts happened.

source.expect: the Proceedings Against the Crown Act, as it read immediately

review.problem: Subsection (3) is expressly subject to subsection (4): section 11 and its extinguishment and dismissal of proceedings also apply to cases started before the Act came into force, so the old Act does not wholly govern them.

items.title: 2019 Act applies to cases started after it came in
items.says: The 2019 Act applies to every proceeding started against the Crown, or a Crown officer, employee or agent, after it came into force, regardless of when the facts took place.

source.expect: regardless of when the facts

items.title: Which law wins if two laws limit Crown liability
items.says: If this Act conflicts with another Act, this Act wins. But if another Act limits the liability of the Crown or its staff, whichever law gives the Crown more protection applies, unless that other Act says otherwise.

source.expect: greater protection against such liability prevails

items.title: Claims under special Acts are not changed
items.says: The Act does not change, and gives way to, certain special laws, including the Expropriations Act, the Public Transportation and Highway Improvement Act, the Land Titles Assurance Fund rules, the Motor Vehicle Accident Claims Act, the Workplace Safety and Insurance Act, 1997, and tax statutes. Claims under those laws follow their own rules.

source.expect: This Act does not affect and is subject to

items.title: A statutory right only works against the Crown if that law binds the Crown
items.says: A right given by another Act cannot be enforced against the Crown under this Act if the Act that gives the right does not bind the Crown.

source.expect: if the Act that confers the right does not bind the Crown

items.title: Municipal Act, 2001
items.says: Under the Municipal Act, 2001, a municipality must keep a highway or bridge it has jurisdiction over in a state of repair that is reasonable in the circumstances, and the same section sets a 10-day written notice for claims about a failure to repair.

source.expect: keep it in a state of repair that is reasonable

review.problem: Section 44 covers the road and bridge repair duty and the 10-day notice, but not which municipalities the Act governs, staff good-faith protection, or the power to quash by-laws, which are elsewhere in the Act.

items.title: City of Toronto Act, 2006
items.says: For the City of Toronto, the City of Toronto Act, 2006 sets out the same road and bridge repair duty, the sidewalk snow-and-ice rule and the 10-day notice that the Municipal Act sets for other municipalities.

source.expect: The City shall keep a highway or bridge

items.title: Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019
items.says: Under the Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019, a police service board is liable for the acts or omissions of members of its police service committed in the course of their employment, and the municipality is responsible for those liabilities.

source.expect: A police service board is liable for the acts or omissions

review.problem: Section 47 (1) is only about a police service board's liability for its members' acts in the course of employment; the general description of the Act and the Law Enforcement Complaints Agency complaints process are not in s. 47.

items.title: Judicial Review Procedure Act
items.says: This Act lets a person ask a court to review a decision made under a statutory power, for example by a government official, a tribunal or a municipal body, and to set it aside if it was made unlawfully or unfairly.

source.citation: Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1
source.expect: application for judicial review

items.title: Statutory Powers Procedure Act
items.says: The Statutory Powers Procedure Act applies, subject to listed exceptions such as courts, to a tribunal using a statutory power of decision under an Ontario Act where the law requires it to hold a hearing, or offer the parties one, before deciding.

source.expect: an opportunity for a hearing before making a decision

review.problem: Section 3 (1) only says when the Act applies; the hearing rules listed (notice, evidence, cross-examination, written decisions) are in other sections.

items.title: Ombudsman Act
items.says: The Ombudsman of Ontario is an independent officer of the Legislature who investigates complaints about the administration of provincial government bodies and, since 2016, municipalities, school boards and universities.

source.citation: Ombudsman Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.6
source.expect: investigate any decision or recommendation made or any act done or omitted

items.title: Limitations Act, 2002
items.says: Most claims against the government, cities and police have the same basic time limit as any other claim: two years from the day the claim was discovered.

source.expect: after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered

items.title: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1)
items.says: Anyone whose Charter rights or freedoms were infringed or denied may apply to a court of competent jurisdiction for the remedy the court considers appropriate and just in the circumstances.

source.expect: such remedy as the court considers appropriate and just

review.problem: Section 24 (1) does not mention damages; it speaks only of the remedy the court considers appropriate and just.

items.title: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act (Canada)
items.says: Claims against the federal government (for example the RCMP, Canada Border Services Agency or Correctional Service Canada) fall under the federal Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, not the Ontario Act. The federal Crown is liable for torts committed by its servants as if it were a person.

source.citation: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50
source.expect: The Crown is liable for the damages for which

items.title: Ministry of the Attorney General Act, s. 8
items.says: A person who was prosecuted cannot sue the Crown Attorney or provincial prosecutor personally for what they did in the prosecution. The claim is brought against the Attorney General of Ontario instead.

source.expect: No action or other proceeding for damages shall be commenced by

items.title: Victims' Bill of Rights, 1995 creates no right to sue
items.says: The Victims' Bill of Rights, 1995 sets out principles for how victims of crime are to be treated by justice officials. It states that no new cause of action, appeal, claim or other remedy comes from those principles.

source.expect: No new cause of action, right of appeal, claim or other remedy

items.title: Canadian Victims Bill of Rights creates no right to damages
items.says: Under the Canadian Victims Bill of Rights, no cause of action or right to damages arises when a right under that Act is infringed or denied.

source.expect: No cause of action or right to damages arises

review.problem: Section 28 only says no cause of action or right to damages arises; the list of rights and the complaint remedy are in other sections.

items.title: Special Investigations Unit Act, 2019
items.says: The Special Investigations Unit (SIU) is a civilian agency that investigates police and certain other officials when an incident involves death, serious injury, firearm discharge at a person, or an allegation of sexual assault. It decides whether criminal charges are laid; it does not award compensation.

source.citation: Special Investigations Unit Act, 2019, S.O. 2019, c. 1, Sched. 5
source.expect: serious injury

items.title: When the Ontario Crown is liable in tort
items.says: The Crown is liable in tort as if it were a person for: a tort committed by its officer, employee or agent; a breach of duty that comes with owning, occupying or controlling property; a breach of an employment duty owed to its own officers or employees; and liability under an Act, regulation or by-law.

source.expect: all the liabilities in tort to which it would be liable if it were a person

items.title: The Crown is liable only through the acts of its people
items.says: The Crown's liability for torts committed by its officers, employees or agents does not extend to a tort that does not come from the acts or omissions of one of its officers, employees or agents.

source.expect: not attributable to the acts or omissions of an officer

review.problem: Section 8 (2) limits only clause 8 (1) (a) (torts of officers, employees or agents); the item states it as a rule for every kind of Crown tort liability.

items.title: If the employee is protected, so is the Crown
items.says: When a law protects a Crown officer, employee or agent from liability, the Crown gets the same protection. No claim may be brought against the Crown for an act if a tort claim for that act could not be brought against the officer, employee or agent.

source.expect: applies to the same extent and in the same manner with respect to the Crown

items.title: Contribution and indemnity apply to the Crown
items.says: The rules on sharing liability among wrongdoers (contribution and indemnity) apply to the Crown as if it were a person, so the Crown can be added as a party to share fault or can claim against others.

source.expect: enforceable by and against the Crown

items.title: Crown not liable for agencies, Crown corporations, funded bodies or contractors
items.says: The Crown is not liable for torts committed by Crown agencies, Crown corporations, transfer payment recipients, or independent contractors providing services to the Crown.

source.expect: The Crown is not liable for torts committed by

review.problem: Section 9 (1) does not list examples of transfer payment recipients and does not say a claim is brought against the body itself.

items.title: Who counts as a transfer payment recipient
items.says: A transfer payment recipient is anyone who receives provincial funding to deliver services to the public, including a municipality, a public or private hospital, a school board, a university or college, a children's aid society and a long-term care home.

source.expect: transfer payment recipient

items.title: Good-faith law enforcement and judicial acts
items.says: The Act does not make the Crown answerable for anything done in good faith to enforce the criminal law or the penal provisions of an Act, or for anything done by someone carrying out judicial duties or executing judicial process.

source.expect: anything done in good faith in the enforcement of the criminal

items.title: No negligence claim for making laws
items.says: No cause of action exists against the Crown or its staff for negligence in legislative work, such as preparing a bill, passing an Act or making a regulation.

source.expect: duties or functions of a legislative nature

items.title: No negligence claim for good-faith regulatory decisions
items.says: When a person is harmed by the act or omission of someone who was the subject of a regulatory decision, no cause of action arises against the Crown or its officers, employees or agents for negligence in making that decision in good faith (s. 11 (2)), or for negligence in a purported failure to make one (s. 11 (3)).

source.expect: in respect of a regulatory decision made in good faith

review.problem: Subsection 11 (2) covers regulatory decisions made in good faith; the failure-to-make branch is in s. 11 (3) and has no good-faith condition, and neither subsection gives licensing or inspection as examples.

items.title: No negligence claim for good-faith policy decisions
items.says: No cause of action arises against the Crown or its officers, employees or agents for negligence in making a decision in good faith about a policy matter, or for negligence in a purported failure to make such a decision. Section 11 (5) lists what a policy matter includes, and s. 11 (9) keeps common-law defences and immunities available.

source.expect: in the making of a decision in good faith respecting a policy matter

review.problem: Subsection 11 (4) does not define policy matters or preserve common-law defences; those are in s. 11 (5) and (9) of the same section, but 'delivering and ending programs' paraphrases (5) loosely and the cited pinpoint alone does not carry them.

items.title: What counts as a policy matter
items.says: A policy matter includes creating or changing a program and who is eligible for it, funding it or cutting its funding, how it is carried out (including by others) and how closely the Crown supervises it, and ending it.

source.expect: a policy matter includes

items.title: Barred claims are treated as dismissed
items.says: A proceeding about a matter covered by these immunities cannot be brought or continued, and is deemed dismissed without costs on the day the cause of action was extinguished.

source.expect: deemed to have been dismissed, without costs

items.title: Nelson (City) v. Marchi: policy versus operational decisions
items.says: The Supreme Court explained how to tell an immune core policy decision (based on social, economic and political factors, made in good faith and not irrational) from operational conduct, which can lead to negligence liability.

source.expect: economic, social and political factors

items.title: Cooper v. Hobart: when a public body owes a duty of care
items.says: The Supreme Court set out the test for a duty of care in negligence: first, whether the harm was reasonably foreseeable and the parties were in a relationship of proximity, which together give a prima facie duty of care; second, whether any residual policy considerations outside that relationship negate the duty.

source.expect: prima facie duty of care

review.problem: Paragraph 30 sets out the two-stage Anns test but does not say it is often applied to regulators and public bodies.

items.title: No seizure of Crown property
items.says: Nothing in the Act authorizes a proceeding in rem for a claim against the Crown, or the seizure, attachment, arrest, detention or sale of any Crown property.

source.expect: seizure, attachment, arrest, detention or sale of any property of the Crown

review.problem: Section 5 says only that nothing in this Act authorizes a proceeding in rem or the seizure of Crown property; it does not prohibit them outright.

items.title: Notice of claim to the Crown at least 60 days before suing
items.says: Before starting any proceeding that claims damages against the Ontario Crown, the claimant must serve the Crown with a written notice of claim at least 60 days before the case is started. The notice must give enough detail to identify the occasion the claim arose from, and is served on the Crown Law Office (Civil Law).

source.expect: at least 60 days before the commencement of the proceeding

items.title: The Attorney General may ask for more details
items.says: After a notice of claim is served, the Attorney General may require more particulars needed to investigate the claim.

source.expect: may require such additional particulars

items.title: Limitation extended if the 60 days run past it
items.says: If the notice is served before the limitation period runs out, but the 60-day wait ends after it, the limitation period is extended to the end of the seventh day after the 60-day period ends.

source.expect: the last instant of the seventh day following the end of the 60-day period

items.title: 10-day notice for claims about Crown property
items.says: For a claim based on the Crown's duty as owner, occupier or controller of property (for example a fall in a government building), the notice of claim must be served no later than 10 days after the event.

source.expect: no later than 10 days after the occurrence of the event

items.title: No notice needed for a counterclaim or set-off
items.says: The notice requirement does not apply to a counterclaim, crossclaim or set-off against the Crown.

source.expect: does not apply with respect to a counterclaim, crossclaim

items.title: No notice means the claim is a nullity
items.says: If the required notice was not given, a proceeding brought without it is a nullity for that claim from the time it was brought.

source.expect: renders a proceeding brought without such notice a nullity

items.title: The Crown may settle a claim after notice
items.says: The Minister of Finance pays amounts the Crown owes under a settlement of a claim that was the subject of a notice of claim, or of an anticipated proceeding, as well as under final court orders.

source.expect: the subject of a notice of claim under section 18

items.title: How to name the Ontario government
items.says: In a proceeding to which the Ontario Crown is a party, the Crown is named as "His Majesty the King in right of Ontario" (in French, "Sa Majesté du chef de l'Ontario").

source.expect: His Majesty the King in right of Ontario

review.problem: Section 14 sets how the Crown is designated but says nothing about whether a ministry may be named as a separate party.

items.title: Serving the Crown
items.says: A document that must be served personally on the Crown is served by leaving a copy with an employee at the Crown Law Office (Civil Law) of the Ministry of the Attorney General.

source.expect: Crown Law Office (Civil Law)

items.title: Serving the Crown in Small Claims Court
items.says: In Small Claims Court, personal service on the Ontario Crown is made in the way set out in section 15 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019.

source.expect: in accordance with section 15

items.title: The usual court rules apply
items.says: Except where the Act says otherwise, the ordinary rules of court apply to a proceeding to which the Crown is a party.

source.expect: the rules of court apply with respect to a proceeding

review.problem: Section 13 (1) says only that the rules of court apply; the court's power to make any order it could make between persons is in s. 12, not s. 13.

items.title: No petition of right is needed
items.says: The old petition of right procedure is abolished. A claim against the Crown is brought as of right, as an ordinary proceeding, but limitation periods still apply.

source.expect: petition of right is abolished

items.title: Starting a Superior Court action: statement of claim
items.says: Except in listed cases such as a notice of action, an action in the Superior Court of Justice is started with a statement of claim (Form 14A, or 14B for mortgage actions).

source.expect: is a statement of claim (Form 14A

review.problem: Rule 14.03 (1) names the statement of claim as the originating process but says nothing about issuing or serving it, and it also lists exceptions.

items.title: Starting quickly with a notice of action
items.says: Where there is not enough time to prepare a statement of claim before a deadline, an action may be started with a notice of action (Form 14C), followed by a statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days.

source.expect: an action may be commenced by the issuing of a notice of action

items.title: Starting in Small Claims Court
items.says: A Small Claims Court action is started by filing a plaintiff's claim (Form 7A) with the clerk, with a copy for each defendant (no copies are needed if the claim is filed electronically).

source.expect: filing a plaintiff's claim (Form 7A)

review.problem: Rule 7.01 (1) says how an action starts but does not state the $50,000 limit, the exclusion of interest and costs, or that claims against the Crown, cities and police boards can be brought there.

items.title: Small Claims Court money limit
items.says: The maximum amount of a claim in the Small Claims Court is $50,000.

review.problem: Section 1 (1) of O. Reg. 626/00 sets the $50,000 maximum but says nothing about interest and costs being excluded.

items.title: Defence due 20 days after service (Superior Court)
items.says: A defendant served in Ontario delivers a statement of defence (Form 18A) within 20 days after being served with the statement of claim.

source.expect: within twenty days after service of the statement of claim

items.title: Defence due 20 days after service (Small Claims)
items.says: In Small Claims Court, a defendant who disputes the claim serves and files a defence (Form 9A) within 20 days of being served.

source.expect: within 20 days of being served with the claim

items.title: No default judgment against the Crown without leave
items.says: The Crown cannot be noted in default, and default judgment cannot be entered against it, unless the court grants leave on a motion served on the Crown under section 15.

source.expect: except with leave of the court to be obtained on motion

items.title: Motion to strike a claim that discloses no cause of action
items.says: A party may ask a judge to strike out a pleading because it discloses no reasonable cause of action or defence, or to decide before trial a question of law raised by a pleading where deciding it may dispose of all or part of the action, substantially shorten the trial or save substantial costs.

source.expect: discloses no reasonable cause of action

review.problem: Rule 21.01 (1) does not say government defendants often use it or mention immunity, and it drops the condition that a question of law may be decided only where that may dispose of or shorten the case or save costs.

items.title: Summary judgment
items.says: The court grants summary judgment if there is no genuine issue requiring a trial on a claim or defence.

source.expect: no genuine issue requiring a trial

items.title: Hryniak v. Mauldin: summary judgment
items.says: The Supreme Court held that summary judgment is available where the judge can make the necessary findings of fact and apply the law, and it is a proportionate, quicker and less costly way to reach a just result.

source.expect: a fair and just determination on the merits

items.title: Discovery when the Crown is a party
items.says: The usual discovery rules apply to the Crown as if it were a corporation, with exceptions: the Crown may refuse to produce a document or answer a question on public-interest grounds; an official named by the Deputy Attorney General is examined; and the Crown delivers a signed list of documents instead of an affidavit of documents.

source.expect: in the same manner as if the Crown were a corporation

items.title: Public interest immunity
items.says: The Act does not change the rule of law that allows or requires a document to be withheld, or a question to go unanswered, in a case involving the Crown where disclosure would be injurious to the public interest.

source.expect: would be injurious to the public interest

review.problem: Section 13 (2) only preserves the existing rule of law on public-interest withholding; it does not say the court decides whether the claim holds.

items.title: No discovery of the Crown when it is not a party
items.says: The Act does not make the Crown or its staff subject to documentary discovery or examination for discovery in a case where the Crown is not a party.

source.expect: in a proceeding to which the Crown is not a party

items.title: Trial without a jury
items.says: A trial against the Crown, or against a Crown officer or employee, is heard by a judge alone, without a jury.

source.expect: trial shall be without a jury

items.title: No injunction or specific performance against the Crown
items.says: A court cannot grant an injunction or order specific performance against the Crown, or against an official where the effect would be relief against the Crown. Instead, the court may declare the parties' rights (but not by an interim declaration).

source.expect: grant an injunction or make an order for specific performance

items.title: A declaration of rights instead
items.says: In place of an injunction or specific performance, the court may make an order declaring the rights of the parties. It cannot make an interim or interlocutory declaration.

source.expect: make an order declaratory of the rights of the parties

items.title: Property claims: a declaration, not an order to return
items.says: Where a person claims property from the Crown, the court does not order it returned, but may declare that the person is entitled to the property or its possession.

source.expect: make an order declaring that the claimant is entitled

items.title: Limits on set-off and counterclaim against the Crown
items.says: A person sued by the Crown for taxes, duties or penalties cannot claim set-off or counterclaim. In other Crown proceedings, a set-off or counterclaim is allowed if it relates to a matter run by the same ministry.

source.expect: relates to a matter under the administration of the particular ministry

items.title: Costs
items.says: Subject to any Act or the rules of court, costs are in the court's discretion, and the court decides who pays them and how much. Costs awarded to the Ontario Crown are not disallowed or reduced just because they relate to a salaried Crown lawyer.

source.expect: in the discretion of the court

review.problem: Section 131 makes costs discretionary and says Crown costs are not reduced because a salaried Crown lawyer did the work; it does not say the Crown is ordered to pay costs like any other party or mention offers to settle.

items.title: Offer to settle and its cost consequences
items.says: A plaintiff's written offer to settle made at least seven days before the hearing, which is not withdrawn and not accepted, can change the costs award if the plaintiff's judgment is as good as or better than the offer.

source.expect: at least seven days before the commencement of the hearing

items.title: Offer to settle in Small Claims Court
items.says: Any party may serve an offer to settle on another party, in writing.

source.expect: an offer to settle a claim on the terms specified

items.title: Settlement conference (Small Claims)
items.says: A settlement conference is held in every defended Small Claims Court action, before any trial.

source.expect: A settlement conference shall be held in every defended action

items.title: Discontinuing a claim
items.says: A plaintiff may discontinue all or part of an action against a defendant before the close of pleadings by serving a notice of discontinuance (Form 23A) on every party served with the claim and filing it with proof of service; after the close of pleadings, with leave of the court; or at any time by filing the consent of all parties.

source.expect: a notice of discontinuance (Form 23A)

review.problem: The rule also allows discontinuance at any time by filing the consent of all parties, so leave is not the only route after the close of pleadings.

items.title: Appeal
items.says: An appeal is started by serving a notice of appeal within 30 days after the order appealed from, unless a statute or the rules say otherwise.

source.expect: within 30 days after the making of the order appealed from

items.title: Interest on a judgment against the Crown
items.says: A judgment debt owed by or to the Crown carries interest in the same way as a judgment debt between private persons.

source.expect: bears interest in the same way as a judgment debt

review.problem: Section 26 deals only with interest on a judgment debt; it says nothing about prejudgment interest.

items.title: How the Crown pays a judgment
items.says: Apart from the garnishments allowed by subsections (2) and (3), no execution, attachment or similar process may be issued out of any court against the Crown.

source.expect: no execution or attachment or other process of a similar nature

review.problem: s. 27 (1) only bars execution against the Crown; payment by the Minister of Finance out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund is in s. 28, not the cited provision.

items.title: Payment from the Consolidated Revenue Fund
items.says: The Minister of Finance pays amounts the Crown owes under a final court order that is not subject to appeal, a settlement, or a final tribunal order or arbitration award.

source.expect: pay out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund

items.title: Garnishing money the Crown owes someone else
items.says: A garnishment may be issued against the Crown to catch money it owes a debtor for goods or services, or for support orders, subject to the Wages Act. It only reaches amounts payable by the ministry or unit that was served.

source.expect: A garnishment that is otherwise lawful may issue against the Crown

items.title: Claims of misfeasance or bad faith need leave
items.says: Section 17 applies to any claim against the Crown or a Crown officer or employee that includes misfeasance in public office or another tort based on bad faith in the use of public powers or duties.

source.expect: a tort of misfeasance in public office or a tort based on bad faith

items.title: Motion for leave to proceed; automatic stay
items.says: A case that includes such a claim can go ahead only with the court's leave. Until leave is granted, the whole case is treated as stayed from the moment it is started.

source.expect: may proceed only with leave of the court

items.title: What the claimant files on the leave motion
items.says: On the leave motion, the claimant serves on the defendant (on the Crown, under section 15) and files an affidavit setting out a concise statement of the material facts relied on, and an affidavit of documents listing all relevant documents the claimant has or had.

source.expect: a concise statement of the material facts on which the claimant intends to rely

items.title: The defendant may answer, but need not
items.says: The defendant may serve and file an affidavit with a concise statement of the facts it relies on for its defence, but it is not required to.

source.expect: but is not required to do so

items.title: Limits on cross-examination and discovery on the leave motion
items.says: On the leave motion, only the person who made an affidavit can be examined on it. The defendant is not subject to discovery, inspection of documents or examination for discovery for the motion.

source.expect: other than the maker of the affidavit or prescribed document

items.title: No discovery of the defendant on the leave motion
items.says: The defendant cannot be made to give documentary discovery or be examined for discovery in relation to the leave motion.

source.expect: shall not be subject to discovery or the inspection of documents

items.title: The test for leave
items.says: The court grants leave only if it is satisfied that the proceeding is brought in good faith and that there is a reasonable possibility the misfeasance or bad-faith claim would be resolved in the claimant's favour.

source.expect: there is a reasonable possibility that the claim described

items.title: Each side pays its own costs of the leave motion
items.says: Each party to the leave motion bears its own costs of that motion.

source.expect: shall bear its own costs of the motion

items.title: If leave is granted
items.says: Granting leave lifts the stay, and the case continues as an ordinary proceeding.

source.expect: lifts the stay of the proceeding

items.title: If leave is refused
items.says: If leave is not granted, the proceeding is a nullity. If the case also has other claims, only the misfeasance or bad-faith claim is a nullity, and the stay is lifted for the rest.

source.expect: the proceeding is rendered a nullity

items.title: The Crown may waive the leave requirement
items.says: The Crown may give the claimant written notice that it waives the need for leave, at any time before the leave motion is heard, even before a case is started. If it waives after the case starts, the stay is lifted once notice is given, and the Crown tells the court in writing.

source.expect: the Crown may waive the application of subsection (2)

items.title: When and how the waiver takes effect
items.says: The Crown may waive at any time before the leave motion is heard. If it does so after the case is started, the stay is lifted when the claimant receives notice, and the Crown must notify the court in writing.

source.expect: the stay of the proceeding is lifted once notice of the waiver

items.title: Leave not needed when the Crown is the claimant
items.says: Section 17 does not apply when the Crown itself is the claimant.

source.expect: This section does not apply if the claimant is the Crown

items.title: Older cases under the former section 17
items.says: Cases where a leave motion was brought before July 8, 2020 continue under the old version of section 17. Cases brought before that date without leave were a nullity for the misfeasance claim, but for limitation purposes count as started when they were brought.

source.expect: For the purposes of any applicable limitation period

items.title: Claim about a prosecutor is brought against the Attorney General
items.says: A person who was prosecuted and wants damages for something a Crown Attorney or provincial prosecutor did in the prosecution brings the case against the Attorney General of Ontario, who stands in the prosecutor's place and may be found liable instead.

source.expect: the Attorney General stands in the place of the person

items.title: Notice and procedure rules for claims against the Attorney General
items.says: The 60-day notice of claim, the limitation extension, the discovery rules, trial without a jury and payment rules of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, 2019 apply to a claim against the Attorney General under section 8.

source.expect: subsections 18 (1) to (3) and sections 19, 20 and 28

items.title: Only claims that could have been brought against the prosecutor
items.says: A claim may be brought against the Attorney General under section 8 only if it could have been brought against the prosecutor but for the immunity.

source.expect: could have been brought against a person referred to

items.title: Misfeasance in public office: what must be shown
items.says: A claimant must show that a public officer engaged in deliberate and unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions, and was aware that the conduct was unlawful and apt to injure the claimant, plus the usual elements of any tort: the conduct caused the harm, and the harm is compensable.

source.expect: deliberate unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions

items.title: Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse

items.title: Two-year limitation period
items.says: Unless the Limitations Act provides otherwise, a proceeding cannot be started after the second anniversary of the day the claim was discovered.

source.expect: after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered

review.problem: Limitations Act s. 4 does not say it applies to claims against the Crown, municipalities and police boards.

items.title: When a claim is discovered
items.says: A claim is discovered on the earlier of the day the person knew, or a reasonable person in their circumstances ought to have known, that the injury happened, that it was caused by an act or omission, that it was the act of the person to be sued, and that a proceeding is an appropriate way to seek a remedy.

source.expect: a proceeding would be an appropriate means to seek to remedy it

items.title: Malicious prosecution: time runs once the prosecution ends
items.says: A claim is discovered on the earlier of the day the person knew, or a reasonable person in their circumstances ought to have known, that the injury, loss or damage occurred, that it was caused by an act or omission of the person to be sued, and that a proceeding is an appropriate way to remedy it. (The favourable-termination element of malicious prosecution needs its own source.)

source.expect: the injury, loss or damage had occurred

review.problem: s. 5 (1) is the general discovery rule; it says nothing about malicious prosecution or a requirement that the prosecution ended in the claimant's favour.

items.title: Time does not run while a person is incapable
items.says: The two-year period does not run while the person with the claim cannot start a proceeding because of a physical, mental or psychological condition and has no litigation guardian.

source.expect: is incapable of commencing a proceeding in respect of the claim

items.title: 15-year ultimate limitation period
items.says: No proceeding may be started more than 15 years after the act or omission the claim is based on, whatever the discovery date, subject to exceptions.

source.expect: after the 15th anniversary of the day on which the act or omission

items.title: No limitation period for sexual assault
items.says: There is no limitation period for a proceeding based on a sexual assault. The same applies to other sexual misconduct where the person was a minor, or the other person had charge of them, was in a position of trust or authority, or they were dependent on that person, and to an assault where the person was a minor, or the two had an intimate relationship, or the person was dependent on the assailant.

source.expect: a proceeding based on a sexual assault

review.problem: s. 16 (1) says nothing about 'public bodies responsible for it'; the closest text, s. 16 (1.3), speaks only of the kinds of claims (negligence, fiduciary duty, vicarious liability), not of public bodies.

items.title: No-limitation rule applies to old events
items.says: The no-limitation rule for sexual assault and related claims applies no matter when the act happened or when an earlier limitation period expired, except for cases already finally dismissed or settled.

source.expect: regardless of the expiry of any previously applicable limitation

items.title: Other laws can change the time limit
items.says: The Limitations Act does not override extensions, suspensions or other changes to time limits made by another Act, such as the Crown notice extension.

source.expect: does not affect the extension, suspension or other variation

items.title: No adding a defendant after the limitation runs out
items.says: Once the limitation period has expired against a person, the claim cannot be pursued by adding that person to an existing case, though a misnamed party can be corrected.

source.expect: shall not be pursued by adding the person as a party

items.title: Where to sue the federal Crown
items.says: A claim against the federal Crown may be brought in the Federal Court or in the superior court of the province (in Ontario, the Superior Court of Justice), which has concurrent jurisdiction.

source.citation: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50
source.expect: the superior court of the province

items.title: Naming and serving the federal Crown
items.says: A proceeding against the federal Crown is brought against the Attorney General of Canada, and is served on the Deputy Attorney General of Canada, as the federal Act and the court rules provide.

source.citation: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50
source.expect: the Attorney General of Canada

items.title: Limitation periods for federal Crown claims
items.says: For a claim against the federal Crown arising in Ontario, the provincial limitation rules (the Limitations Act, 2002) generally apply.

source.citation: Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-50

items.title: Judicial review of federal decisions: 30 days
items.says: A federal board, commission or tribunal's decision is challenged by judicial review in the Federal Court within 30 days after it was first communicated, or a longer time a judge allows.

source.citation: Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7
